title: Negligence, damages and liability
summary: The four elements of negligence, Michigan's comparative fault rule, special, general and punitive damages, and absolute, strict and vicarious liability.
objectives: Name the four elements of negligence and the main defenses
Apply Michigan's comparative fault rule to a damage award
Classify special, general and punitive damages
Tell absolute, strict and vicarious liability apart

scenes.title: Negligence, damages and liability
scenes.subtitle: How the law decides who pays when someone gets hurt
scenes.src: ISO CG 00 01 04 13, Sec. I, Cov. A.1.a

beats.text: Liability coverage, like the CGL, pays sums the insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages. So you need to know how the law decides who's responsible.
beats.say: Liability coverage, like the C G L, pays sums the insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages. So you need to know how the law decides who's responsible.

beats.text: In this lesson: the elements of negligence, Michigan's fault rules, the kinds of damages, and three special kinds of liability.
beats.say: In this lesson: the elements of negligence, Michigan's fault rules, the kinds of damages, and three special kinds of liability.

scenes.title: Four elements of negligence
scenes.hook: Don't Break People's Doors: Duty, Breach, Proximate cause, Damage.
items: Duty: the defendant owed the plaintiff a legal duty of care
Breach: the defendant failed to use reasonable care
Proximate cause: the breach led, foreseeably, to the harm
Damage: the plaintiff suffered actual injury or damage

beats.text: Negligence has four elements, and the plaintiff must prove all four. Here's the hook: Don't Break People's Doors.
beats.say: Negligence has four elements, and the plaintiff must prove all four. Here's the hook: Don't Break People's Doors.

beats.text: Duty: the defendant owed the plaintiff a legal duty of care. Breach: the defendant failed to use reasonable care.
beats.say: Duty: the defendant owed the plaintiff a legal duty of care. Breach: the defendant failed to use reasonable care.

beats.text: Proximate cause: the breach set off a foreseeable chain of events that led to the harm. Damage: an actual injury or loss.
beats.say: Proximate cause: the breach set off a foreseeable chain of events that led to the harm. Damage: an actual injury or loss.

beats.text: Watch out: intent to harm is not an element. On an EXCEPT question, intent is usually the odd one out.
beats.say: Watch out: intent to harm is not an element. On an EXCEPT question, intent is usually the odd one out.

scenes.title: Defenses against negligence
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: contributory negligence; comparative negligence; assumption of risk

columns.name: Contributory negligence
points: Any fault by the plaintiff bars recovery

columns.name: Comparative negligence
points: Damages reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault

columns.name: Assumption of risk
points: Knowingly and voluntarily accepted a known risk
Can't recover for the resulting injury

scenes.tell: Contributory: any fault, nothing. Comparative: you lose your share.

beats.text: These are the general defenses; Michigan's rule comes next. Under the old common-law rule of contributory negligence, any fault by the plaintiff bars recovery. Many states have replaced it.
beats.say: These are the general defenses; Michigan's rule comes next. Under the old common-law rule of contributory negligence, any fault by the plaintiff bars recovery. Many states have replaced it.

beats.text: Under comparative negligence, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault.
beats.say: Under comparative negligence, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault.

beats.text: And under assumption of risk, someone who knowingly and voluntarily accepts a known risk can't recover for the resulting injury.
beats.say: And under assumption of risk, someone who knowingly and voluntarily accepts a known risk can't recover for the resulting injury.

beats.text: In short: contributory means any fault, nothing. Comparative means you lose your share.
beats.say: In short: contributory means any fault, nothing. Comparative means you lose your share.

items.label: Your fault doesn't bar recovery
items.detail: Contributory fault is not a complete bar in Michigan

items.label: Damages drop by your percentage
items.detail: Damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault

items.label: More than 50% at fault
items.detail: Economic damages still reduced; no noneconomic damages awarded

items.label: Auto no-fault suits differ
items.detail: Noneconomic-loss suit: no damages for a party more than 50% at fault

beats.text: In Michigan, a plaintiff's own fault does not bar recovery. Instead, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault.
beats.say: In Michigan, a plaintiff's own fault does not bar recovery. Instead, damages are reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault.

beats.text: But if the plaintiff's fault is greater than everyone else's combined, so more than 50%, economic damages are still reduced, and noneconomic damages, like pain and suffering, are not awarded.
beats.say: But if the plaintiff's fault is greater than everyone else's combined, so more than fifty percent, economic damages are still reduced, and noneconomic damages, like pain and suffering, are not awarded.

beats.text: Auto no-fault suits for noneconomic loss use a different rule: a party more than 50% at fault recovers nothing.
beats.say: Auto no-fault suits for noneconomic loss use a different rule: a party more than fifty percent at fault recovers nothing.

scenes.title: Working the Michigan rule
scenes.src: MCL 600.2958; MCL 600.2959 (method as in question core-026)

beats.text: Let's work one. A Michigan plaintiff proves $100,000 of economic damages and is found 30% at fault. What does the plaintiff recover?
beats.say: Let's work one. A Michigan plaintiff proves one hundred thousand dollars of economic damages and is found thirty percent at fault. What does the plaintiff recover?

beats.text: First, the reduction: 30% of $100,000 is $30,000.
beats.say: First, the reduction: thirty percent of one hundred thousand dollars is thirty thousand dollars.

beats.text: So the plaintiff recovers $70,000. Under the old contributory rule, the answer would be zero.
beats.say: So the plaintiff recovers seventy thousand dollars. Under the old contributory rule, the answer would be zero.

scenes.q: In a Michigan general negligence suit, the plaintiff is found exactly 50% at fault. What happens to her noneconomic damages, such as pain and suffering?
scenes.why: Michigan cuts off noneconomic damages only when the plaintiff's fault is more than 50%. At exactly 50%, they are reduced by her share.

beats.text: Here's a trap. A Michigan plaintiff is found exactly 50% at fault. What happens to her noneconomic damages? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Here's a trap. A Michigan plaintiff is found exactly fifty percent at fault. What happens to her noneconomic damages? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: They're reduced by 50%, not barred. The cutoff applies only when the plaintiff is more than 50% at fault, and 50 is not more than 50.
reveal.say: They're reduced by fifty percent, not barred. The cutoff applies only when the plaintiff is more than fifty percent at fault, and fifty is not more than fifty.

scenes.title: Kinds of damages
scenes.src: IRMI glossary: compensatory, special, general, punitive damages; Gilbert v DaimlerChrysler (Mich 2004), via IADC compendium
scenes.hook: Special = Spreadsheet (bills you can add up). General = Gut (pain and suffering). Punitive = Punish. In Michigan, Punish needs Permission from the Legislature.
items: Special: measurable losses like medical bills, lost wages, loss of use
General: a subjective award for pain and suffering
Punitive: beyond compensation, to punish wanton or willful conduct
Michigan: punitive only when the Legislature expressly authorizes it

beats.text: Now, damages. Compensatory damages make amends for the actual loss, and they come in two types. Special equals Spreadsheet. General equals Gut.
beats.say: Now, damages. Compensatory damages make amends for the actual loss, and they come in two types. Special equals Spreadsheet. General equals Gut.

beats.text: Special damages are losses you can add up: medical bills, lost wages, loss of use. General damages are a subjective award for pain and suffering.
beats.say: Special damages are losses you can add up: medical bills, lost wages, loss of use. General damages are a subjective award for pain and suffering.

beats.text: Punitive damages go beyond compensation, to punish wanton or willful conduct.
beats.say: Punitive damages go beyond compensation, to punish wanton or willful conduct.

beats.text: In Michigan, punish needs permission. Punitive damages are generally not recoverable unless the Legislature expressly authorizes them.
beats.say: In Michigan, punish needs permission. Punitive damages are generally not recoverable unless the Legislature expressly authorizes them.

scenes.q: A jury awards a shopper who slipped in a store $25,000 for lost wages and $60,000 for pain and suffering. Which part is general damages?
scenes.why: Pain and suffering is a subjective award, so it is general damages. Lost wages can be added up, so they are special. Both are compensatory.

beats.text: Quick check. A jury awards a shopper who slipped in a store $25,000 for lost wages and $60,000 for pain and suffering. Which part is general damages? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Quick check. A jury awards a shopper who slipped in a store twenty five thousand dollars for lost wages and sixty thousand dollars for pain and suffering. Which part is general damages? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: The $60,000 for pain and suffering. It's a subjective award, so it's general. The lost wages add up, so they're special. Both are compensatory.
reveal.say: The sixty thousand dollars for pain and suffering. It's a subjective award, so it's general. The lost wages add up, so they're special. Both are compensatory.

scenes.title: Absolute, strict and vicarious liability
scenes.src: Restatement (2d) Torts §§519-520; IRMI glossary: strict liability; vicarious liability; LII Wex

columns.name: Strict
points: Classic case: maker or seller of a defective, dangerous product

columns.name: Vicarious
points: Employer for employee in the scope of employment

scenes.tell: Exam convention: blasting is absolute, defective products are strict, someone else's act is vicarious.

beats.text: Absolute liability applies to ultrahazardous activities, like blasting or keeping wild animals. Being careful is no defense.
beats.say: Absolute liability applies to ultrahazardous activities, like blasting or keeping wild animals. Being careful is no defense.

beats.text: Strict liability is imposed without regard to fault. The classic example is the maker or seller of a defective, dangerous product.
beats.say: Strict liability is imposed without regard to fault. The classic example is the maker or seller of a defective, dangerous product.

beats.text: Vicarious liability makes one party liable for someone else's acts, like an employer for an employee acting in the scope of employment. It can also apply to partners, independent contractors and children.
beats.say: Vicarious liability makes one party liable for someone else's acts, like an employer for an employee acting in the scope of employment. It can also apply to partners, independent contractors and children.

beats.text: Legal sources often use absolute and strict interchangeably. These are the generic exam definitions, not Michigan product law: blasting is absolute, defective products are strict.
beats.say: Legal sources often use absolute and strict interchangeably. These are the generic exam definitions, not Michigan product law: blasting is absolute, defective products are strict.

scenes.q: A landscaping company's employee, while mowing a customer's lawn, carelessly throws a rock through a neighbor's window. The company is held liable. This is:
scenes.why: The company is liable for its employee's act within the scope of employment. That's vicarious liability.

beats.text: Last one. A landscaping company's employee, mowing a customer's lawn, carelessly throws a rock through a neighbor's window. The company is held liable. What kind of liability is that? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Last one. A landscaping company's employee, mowing a customer's lawn, carelessly throws a rock through a neighbor's window. The company is held liable. What kind of liability is that? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: Vicarious liability. The company is liable for its employee's act in the scope of employment. Nothing here is ultrahazardous or a defective product.
reveal.say: Vicarious liability. The company is liable for its employee's act in the scope of employment. Nothing here is ultrahazardous or a defective product.

items: Negligence: duty, breach, proximate cause, damage. No intent needed
Michigan: fault reduces damages; over 50% loses noneconomic damages
Special damages add up; general damages are pain and suffering
Michigan punitive damages need express legislative authority
Absolute: blasting. Strict: defective products. Vicarious: via others

beats.text: To recap: negligence needs duty, breach, proximate cause and damage. In Michigan, your fault reduces your damages, and over 50% costs you noneconomic damages.
beats.say: To recap: negligence needs duty, breach, proximate cause and damage. In Michigan, your fault reduces your damages, and over fifty percent costs you noneconomic damages.

beats.text: Special damages add up; general damages are pain and suffering. Michigan punitive damages need the Legislature's permission. And absolute, strict and vicarious liability each have their classic case.
beats.say: Special damages add up; general damages are pain and suffering. Michigan punitive damages need the Legislature's permission. And absolute, strict and vicarious liability each have their classic case.
